poles: Living wage / no one working full time should be poor
Price floors kill jobs / the ladder's first rung gets cut off

reader_anchor.opening_prose: You are seven years old. Your mother gives you a dollar and sends you to the corner store for a loaf of bread. You run the whole way because you want to get back before the cartoon starts. You hand the dollar to the man behind the counter. He hands you the bread and a nickel back. You do not count the nickel. You do not ask where the other 95 cents went. You just take the bread and run home. The bread is warm. You eat two slices with butter and never think about the nickel again. That nickel was the entire profit margin on that loaf. The man behind the counter kept the store open on nickels. You never knew. You never had to know. But someone always knows. Someone always counts the nickels. And when the law says the loaf must cost a dime more, the man behind the counter does not raise the price. He stops selling bread. Or he stops hiring the kid who runs the bread to the register. The kid never sees the decision. The kid just stops getting the dollar. That is the fight. You have been in it since before you could read a price tag. The quiet theft was this: you were trained to see only the wage, never the margin. You were trained to think the price floor only lifts boats. You were never shown the boat that gets sunk because the floor rose too fast. We are here to give that sight back.
reader_anchor.universal_experience: Buying something as a child with exact change and not thinking about the store's margin
reader_anchor.checkable_detail: You did not count the change. You took the item and ran. You never asked where the rest of the money went.
reader_anchor.quiet_theft: You were trained to see only the wage, never the margin that makes the wage possible.
reader_anchor.embodiment_note: The child's experience of buying bread embodies the fight's core distinction: the wage is visible, the margin that sustains the job is invisible, and the fight is about which one gets protected when they collide.

poles.label: Living wage pole
poles.steelman: No person who works full time should live in poverty. Work is the primary legitimate path to subsistence in this economy. If the market wage for a job is below subsistence, the job is not a real job—it is a subsidy from the worker to the employer. The employer is extracting labor at a price that forces the worker to rely on public assistance, which means taxpayers are subsidizing the employer's profitability. A living wage forces the employer to internalize the full cost of labor. It restores the dignity of work. It reduces poverty, inequality, and dependence on welfare. The evidence from multiple city-level increases shows that moderate minimum wage increases do not cause significant job loss. The fear of job destruction is a lobbyist's myth.
poles.accusation_against_others: The price-floor pole forces workers to subsidize employer profitability through poverty wages, making taxpayers cover the difference via food stamps and Medicaid.
poles.accusation_is_true_because: When the wage is below subsistence, the worker cannot cover rent, food, and healthcare. The gap is filled by public assistance. Taxpayers—who did not create the damage of low wages—eat the cost of the worker's survival. The employer offloads labor cost onto the public ledger.

axiom_autopsy.load_bearing_premise: A wage floor set above market equilibrium does not reduce employment because employers can absorb the cost from profits or pass it to prices without reducing labor demand.
axiom_autopsy.self_application: The living wage pole requires that employers have slack (profits, price flexibility) to absorb the wage increase without cutting jobs. But if that slack exists, then the employer could have voluntarily paid a living wage all along. The pole's own premise—that employers can absorb the cost—implies that the employer's failure to pay a living wage was not a market constraint but a choice. If it was a choice, then the pole's moral case rests on forcing a choice the employer could have made freely, which collapses the distinction between coercion and persuasion. The premise that slack exists is also falsified for marginal firms: if slack is universal, no firm fails from wage increases, which is false.
axiom_autopsy.one_question_test: Name one small business in your town that would survive a $5/hour wage increase without cutting hours or raising prices.

poles.label: Price floor pole
poles.steelman: A minimum wage is a price floor on labor. Price floors above market equilibrium create a surplus of labor—unemployment. The workers who keep their jobs get higher pay, but the workers at the margin—the least skilled, the youngest, the most disadvantaged—lose their jobs entirely. The ladder's first rung is cut off. The evidence from Seattle and other cities shows that high minimum wages reduce hours for low-wage workers. The policy helps insiders at the expense of outsiders. It is a transfer from the jobless poor to the employed poor, with the employer and consumer caught in the middle. The only sustainable path out of poverty is skill acquisition and economic growth, not a wage mandate that destroys the entry-level jobs that provide that first step.
poles.accusation_against_others: The living wage pole prices marginal workers out of the labor market, making the most vulnerable workers—teenagers, immigrants, the disabled—eat the cost of higher wages for insiders.
poles.accusation_is_true_because: When the wage floor is set above the productivity of a marginal worker, the employer cannot hire that worker at the mandated wage. The worker loses the job opportunity entirely. That worker—who did not create the damage of low wages—eats the full cost of the policy in lost income and lost experience.

axiom_autopsy.load_bearing_premise: Any wage floor above market equilibrium necessarily reduces employment for marginal workers, and this job loss is worse than the poverty the floor aims to cure.
axiom_autopsy.self_application: The price floor pole requires that the market wage is the correct measure of a worker's value and that any interference destroys value. But the market wage for a janitor in 1938 was $0.25/hour. Applied consistently, the premise that market wages are optimal would forbid any minimum wage, including the one that ended sweatshops. The premise also requires that the alternative to a minimum wage—unregulated wages—produces better outcomes for marginal workers. But unregulated wages can fall below subsistence, which creates the poverty the living wage pole objects to. The premise that job loss is always worse than poverty wages is an empirical claim that fails for workers who are already in poverty: losing a poverty wage job may be no worse than keeping it. The premise treats 'having a job' as an absolute good, ignoring the quality of that job.
axiom_autopsy.one_question_test: Name one industry where the market wage in 2023 was below $7.25/hour and workers in that industry were better off than if they had been paid $15/hour and lost their jobs.

ledger.D_definition: The deficit between the market wage for low-productivity labor and a subsistence standard of living (e.g., $15/hour vs. actual productivity of ~$10/hour for some workers). D = $5/hour per affected worker, times 20 million workers = $100 billion/year estimated gap.
ledger.D_is_real_evidence: 20 million U.S. workers earn below $15/hour; many rely on public assistance. The gap between earnings and basic living costs is measurable via the Supplemental Poverty Measure and SNAP enrollment data.
ledger.victim_class: Low-wage workers who cannot cover basic living costs from their wages, and taxpayers who subsidize those workers via public assistance.
ledger.causal_class: Diffuse. Employers paying below-subsistence wages are the proximate cause, but the deeper cause is the market valuation of low-skill labor below subsistence, which is a structural feature of the economy, not a conspiracy. Agency is partial: some employers can pay more, some cannot.

per_pole_transfers.T_A: $100 billion/year transferred from employers and consumers to low-wage workers via higher wages
per_pole_transfers.T_B: $100 billion/year cost imposed on employers (higher labor costs) and consumers (higher prices)
per_pole_transfers.W_note: Workers voluntarily accept higher wages; employers are forced to pay. No voluntary participation by employers.
per_pole_transfers.who_eats_deficit: Marginal workers priced out of employment (the surplus labor) eat the deficit in lost jobs and income.

per_pole_transfers.T_A: $0 transferred to low-wage workers (wages remain at market)
per_pole_transfers.W_note: Employers voluntarily pay market wages; workers are forced to accept them. No voluntary participation by workers.
per_pole_transfers.who_eats_deficit: Low-wage workers and taxpayers eat the deficit via poverty wages and public assistance subsidies.

clear_win.statement: The minimum wage fight is a seating argument on the J + M = 1 line. Both poles' accusations are true simultaneously: the living wage pole forces marginal workers to eat the cost of higher wages for insiders; the price floor pole forces workers and taxpayers to eat the cost of poverty wages for employers. No position on the line closes the ledger—someone who did not create the damage always eats the deficit. The only exit is a voluntary external cost-bearer who absorbs the gap between market productivity and subsistence without destroying jobs or forcing poverty.
derivation_steps: 1. Define D = $5/hour gap between subsistence wage ($15) and marginal worker productivity ($10).
2. Living wage pole sets T_A = $5/hour (transfer to workers), T_B = $5/hour (cost on employers). J = 1, M = 0. Marginal workers priced out eat the deficit in lost jobs.
3. Price floor pole sets T_A = $0, T_B = $0. J = 0, M = 1. Workers and taxpayers eat the deficit in poverty wages and subsidies.
4. Both accusations are true: each pole makes someone who did not create the damage eat the cost.
5. No position on the line (0 <= J <= 1) avoids this: any J > 0 prices out some marginal workers; any J < 1 leaves some workers in poverty.
6. The line is invariant. The fight cannot be resolved by adjusting the wage level—it can only be relocated along the line.
7. Resolution requires a voluntary external cost-bearer who absorbs the $5/hour gap without imposing cost on employers or workers.
clear_win.dinner_table_sentence: Every minimum wage debate just picks who eats the gap between what labor is worth and what life costs.
clear_win.why_undeniable: Both sides' core accusations are empirically verified: job loss from minimum wage increases is documented (Seattle study, CBO estimates), and poverty wages requiring public subsidies are documented (UCSF study, USDA data). A hostile reader must concede both are true, which proves the line exists.

structures: Worker-owned cooperatives that set wages based on revenue sharing, not market rates
Employer-sponsored wage supplementation programs (e.g., profit-sharing, housing subsidies)
Community-supported wage funds (voluntary pools that top up wages for specific workers)
Universal basic income or negative income tax (relocates the deficit to taxpayers, still on the line)
proximate.honest_limit: All proximate structures relocate the cost voluntarily and visibly, but they do not retire the deficit. The altruism lemma holds: internal love/restitution moves the cost along the line; it does not eliminate the need for someone to bear it.

ultimate.configuration: A voluntary external cost-bearer who (1) is neither worker nor employer nor conscripted taxpayer, (2) acts voluntarily, (3) absorbs the full D = $5/hour gap, (4) has capacity to absorb without being destroyed, (5) preserves truth (damage acknowledged, not denied).
ultimate.candidate: The historical candidate identified by the framework is the voluntary substitutionary cost-bearer of Part 13—structurally, the one who absorbs the deficit without coercion and without requiring anyone else to pay. The door opens from the reader's side only.
ultimate.door_note: No coercion. The reader must choose to step into the role of the external cost-bearer or accept that the line remains. The framework names the candidate; it does not compel acceptance.

anti_gaming_audit.blind_label: pass: analysis uses 'employer' and 'worker' without party names; survives actor reversal
anti_gaming_audit.symmetry: pass: win applies regardless of which pole proposed the mechanism
anti_gaming_audit.counterfactual: pass: D (poverty wage gap) is real absent any minimum wage policy
anti_gaming_audit.radius_consistency: pass: benefits and costs measured at the worker/employer level consistently
anti_gaming_audit.cost_visibility: pass: costs are visible to those paying them (lost jobs, poverty wages)
anti_gaming_audit.no_person_score: pass: actions and positions scored, never souls
anti_gaming_audit.unknowns_tracked: pass: D is estimated with known uncertainty; unknown elasticity of job loss is reported as unknown

falsification.kill_condition_specific: A historical case where a minimum wage increase to subsistence level resulted in zero job loss for marginal workers AND zero reduction in hours AND zero price increases to consumers, with no external subsidy, would break this resolution's claim that marginal workers always eat the deficit.
falsification.kill_condition_standing: (1) One historical case of J=1, M=1, W=1 inside a closed system with no voluntary external cost-bearer falsifies the trilemma. (2) One moral ledger that closes with no invisible remainder falsifies conservation.
